chapters.title: Chapter 5: Funding Gaps, Tax Outflows and Surplus Cash

lessons.title: Where to Park Surplus Cash: Sweep Accounts, Fixed Deposits and Liquid Funds

children.text: Most of this course has dealt with not having enough cash. The opposite problem is real too, and it is handled worse than almost anything else in Indian business finance. Money collects in a current account earning nothing, or it gets locked into a two-year deposit three weeks before advance tax is due, or, worst of all, a company borrows at 11% while holding a fixed deposit at 6.5% and quietly loses the difference every single day.

body.text: Surplus cash is not spare cash. Before parking a rupee anywhere, answer one question: on what date do I need it back? Everything else follows from that answer.

children.text: Sort the Money by Date First
Treasury decisions get easier the moment you stop treating the bank balance as one pool. Split it by when it is needed.

cells: Payroll, suppliers, the 7th, the 15th and the 20th
Advance tax, a capex milestone, a bonus, a seasonal build-up
Maturity matched to the exact date
The cushion against a customer defaulting or a season failing
Safety and quick access, in that order
Expansion, acquisition, or genuinely surplus capital
A board conversation, not a treasury one

body.text: The order of priorities in corporate treasury is safety, then liquidity, then return. Not because return does not matter, but because the downside is asymmetric: an extra 1% on a ₹50 lakh parking gets nobody promoted, and money that is inaccessible on the 20th can bounce a statutory payment.

children.text: The Best Return Is Usually Repaying the Bank
If a business has any working capital borrowing outstanding, that is where surplus cash belongs first, and the arithmetic is not close.

body.text: Borrowing at 11% while holding a deposit at 6.5% loses 4.5 points a year on the overlapping amount, before tax on the interest earned makes it worse. It happens constantly, usually because the deposit is pledged as security, or because a fixed deposit feels like prudence while an overdraft feels like a separate problem. Check for this in your own company before doing anything else in this lesson.

body.title: What is the sweep worth?
body.prompt: A company has ₹25 lakh drawn on a cash credit account at 11% a year, and ₹25 lakh of surplus sitting idle for 90 days. How much interest does it save by using the surplus to reduce the drawn balance for those 90 days, in rupees?
body.explanation: ₹25,00,000 times 11% is ₹2,75,000 a year, and for 90 days that is about ₹67,808. Because cash credit interest is charged on the daily outstanding balance, this saving happens automatically simply by keeping the money in that account rather than a separate current account. No investment decision, no paperwork, no risk.

children.text: Once borrowings are cleared, the choice is about matching the date. These are the options Indian businesses actually use.

cells: Earns nothing. Companies cannot hold savings accounts, so idle balances here are pure loss
Sweep or flexi deposit linked to the account
Break-up rules and minimum sweep amounts vary by bank
Graded exit load if redeemed within 7 days, cut-off timings, and market risk, small but not zero
On maturity, or premature with penalty
Premature withdrawal penalty, and the temptation to over-lock
Requires a demat account and some operational setup
Credit risk is real. Yield above the market is a warning, not an opportunity

body.label: Your company cannot open a savings account
body.context: Savings deposit accounts are not permitted for trading or business concerns, whether a proprietorship, a partnership firm or a company. Business entities use current accounts, which pay no interest, which is exactly why a sweep or flexi deposit arrangement matters: without one, every idle rupee earns zero by default.

body.title: The practical details that catch people out

children.text: Liquid fund transactions are processed against daily cut-offs, commonly 3 pm for redemption on a business day. Miss it and the money moves a day later, which matters when payroll is on the 1st.

SEBI requires a graded exit load on liquid funds for redemptions within 7 days, starting around 0.0070% on day one and tapering to nil from day seven. On ₹1 lakh that is roughly ₹7 on day one, small, but it means liquid funds are not designed for two-day parking.
Redemption is commonly credited on a T+1 basis, subject to the scheme and intervening holidays. Plan around bank holidays, not just weekends.

Breaking a deposit usually means interest at the rate applicable for the period actually run, less a penalty. Laddering several smaller deposits instead of one large one avoids breaking the whole amount for a small need.

Interest and gains are taxable, and TDS may apply to deposit interest. The after-tax return is what should be compared against your borrowing rate. Confirm current treatment with your chartered accountant, since rules for different fund categories have changed in recent years.
None of this is exotic. It is simply the difference between a treasury decision that works on the day you need the money and one that technically earned a slightly better rate.

body.title: The order of priorities
body.textWithBlank: In corporate treasury, the three criteria are applied in this order: safety, liquidity, and then ___.
body.explanation: Return comes last deliberately. Corporate cash exists to meet obligations, so chasing an extra fraction of a percent by accepting credit risk or locking in money inverts the purpose of holding it in the first place.

body.title: Advance tax is due on 15 December
body.question: It is 20 October. You hold ₹9 lakh that must be paid as advance tax on 15 December, and the cash credit account is fully repaid. Where does that money belong?
options: A three-year fixed deposit at the highest available rate, broken early in December
An instrument maturing on or just before 15 December, such as a short deposit or a liquid or overnight fund
An equity mutual fund, since the horizon is nearly two months
Left in the current account, because it will be needed soon anyway
body.explanation: The date is known exactly, so the instrument should mature just before it. A three-year deposit earns a headline rate you will not receive after the premature withdrawal penalty. Equity is inappropriate for money with a fixed near-term obligation, whatever the market is doing. Leaving it in the current account is safe but earns nothing for eight weeks.

body.title: Six crore in the bank and a suggestion from the board
body.scenario: LedgerLoop, the startup from Lesson 4.3, has ₹6 crore in the bank after its seed round, a net burn of ₹50 lakh a month and about 12 months of runway. A board member suggests putting ₹3 crore into an equity mutual fund, pointing out that markets have done well and that the money is "not needed for a year anyway". The founders ask for your view.
body.prompt: How do you respond, and what structure would you propose instead?
body.modelAnswer:
Start with what the money is.
1. This is not surplus capital. It is the operating runway, raised from investors for a stated purpose, and it is the only thing standing between the company and closure. Its job is to be available, not to grow.
2. The horizon is not a year. The horizon is a series of monthly payroll dates starting in 30 days, plus statutory dues, plus whatever the plan accelerates.
3. Equity exposure creates the worst possible correlation: a funding market that turns difficult is usually the same environment in which equity values fall, so the buffer would shrink exactly when the next round gets harder.
Then propose a structure that is defensible and still earns something.
4. Three months of burn, about ₹1.5 crore, in the current account with a sweep or flexi deposit arrangement, available same day.
5. The next three months, about ₹1.5 crore, in overnight or liquid funds or short deposits with staggered maturities.
6. The remaining ₹3 crore laddered across fixed deposits maturing every one to three months, so cash becomes available continuously and nothing needs to be broken early.
7. Match specific known outflows to specific maturities: advance tax dates, the annual insurance and audit fees, any equipment purchase already committed.
Then write the rules down before anything is invested.
8. A one-page treasury policy approved by the board: permitted instruments, maximum tenor, maximum exposure to any single bank or fund house, and who is authorised to move money.
9. Two-person authorisation for every transfer, with the person who initiates not being the person who approves.
10. Monthly reporting to the board of where every rupee sits and when it matures.
And say the hard part plainly.
11. If the company wants investment returns, it should return the capital to investors, who can invest it themselves. A startup is not paid to take market risk with its runway, and no investor has ever been impressed by treasury gains on money raised to build a product.

body.title: Write your one-page treasury policy
steps: Check first whether any borrowing is outstanding, and set the rule that surplus reduces borrowing before it is parked anywhere.
Define the minimum operating float to be kept instantly accessible, in weeks of outflow rather than as a fixed rupee figure.
List every known outflow for the next twelve months with its date, and match instruments to those dates.
Set the permitted instruments explicitly, and state that anything not listed requires board approval.
Set concentration limits: a maximum with any one bank, fund house or issuer.
Set maximum tenor, and require that maturities ladder rather than cluster.
Name the authorised signatories and require dual authorisation, with initiation and approval separated.
Set up a sweep or flexi arrangement on the main current account so that idle balances never earn zero by default.
Report monthly: balances, instruments, maturity dates and the average return earned against the borrowing rate.
Review the policy annually with your chartered accountant or adviser, and after any major change in the business.

cards.definition: An automatic arrangement moving balances above a threshold from the current account into a deposit, and back when needed.
A mutual fund investing in very short-term instruments, typically redeemable on a T plus one basis, with a graded exit load inside 7 days.
Splitting money across deposits maturing at staggered dates, so cash becomes available continuously without breaking anything.
Choosing an instrument that matures on or just before the date the money is needed.
A cap on how much may be placed with any single bank, fund house or issuer.
The written rules on permitted instruments, tenors, limits and authorisations. It exists so decisions are not made under pressure.

points: Sort surplus by the date it is needed: operating float, known outflows, buffer and strategic reserve. The date chooses the instrument.
Repaying working capital borrowing is the best available use of surplus. It returns your full borrowing rate, risk-free and untaxed.
Repaying ₹25 lakh of cash credit and parking ₹15 lakh beat parking all ₹40 lakh by about ₹27,700 over one quarter.
Never borrow at 11% while holding a deposit at 6.5%. That is a 4.5 point loss on the overlap, and it is common.
Businesses cannot hold savings accounts in India, so without a sweep arrangement every idle balance earns exactly nothing.
Safety, then liquidity, then return. Write a one-page treasury policy with instruments, limits and dual authorisation before the money arrives, not after.

body.text: Konkan Ceramics and LedgerLoop are fictional, and the 11% and 6.5% rates are illustrative, not current market rates. This lesson is educational and is not investment advice or a recommendation of any instrument, scheme or institution. Exit loads, cut-off timings, settlement cycles and tax treatment can change and vary by scheme and by taxpayer. Consult your chartered accountant or a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making treasury decisions.
